claim: Protein kinases are crucial to coordinate cellular decisions and therefore their activities are strictly regulated.
source: Protein kinases are crucial to coordinate cellular decisions and therefore their activities are strictly regulated.
evidence: This is a general statement about protein kinases that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Ancestral reconstruction was previously used to determine how CMGC group kinase specificity evolved (Howard et al., 2014).
source: Previously we used ancestral reconstruction to determine how CMGC group kinase specificity evolved (Howard et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous publication.

claim: Kinases switched from high to low autophosphorylation activity at the transition to the inferred ancestor of ERKs 1 and 2.
source: Kinases switched from high to low autophosphorylation activity at the transition to the inferred ancestor of ERKs 1 and 2.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Two synergistic amino acid changes were sufficient to induce the change from high to low autophosphorylation: shortening of the β3-αC loop and mutation of the gatekeeper residue.
source: Two synergistic amino acid changes were sufficient to induce this change: shortening of the β3-αC loop and mutation of the gatekeeper residue.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Restoring the two mutations to their inferred ancestral state led to a loss of dependence of modern ERKs 1 and 2 on the upstream activating kinase MEK in human cells.
source: Restoring these two mutations to their inferred ancestral state led to a loss of dependence of modern ERKs 1 and 2 on the upstream activating kinase MEK in human cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: More than 500 kinases in the human genome comprise ~2% of all protein coding genes.
source: They are one of the largest protein families in eukaryotes (Lahiry et al., 2010); more than 500 kinases in the human genome comprise ~2% of all protein coding genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lahiry et al., 2010.

claim: Inappropriate kinase activation drives most cancers.
source: in particular, inappropriate kinase activation drives most cancers.
evidence: This is a general statement based on established knowledge in cancer biology.

claim: Most serine/threonine kinases and a subset of tyrosine kinases are regulated by phosphorylation of a conserved TxY motif within the activation loop.
source: Most serine/threonine kinases and a subset of tyrosine kinases are regulated by phosphorylation of a conserved TxY motif within this loop.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge in kinase biology.

claim: Phosphorylation of the activation loop affects both substrate binding and the arrangement of catalytic residues (Johnson et al., 1996; Nolen et al., 2004).
source: This phosphorylation affects both substrate binding and the arrangement of catalytic residues (Johnson et al., 1996; Nolen et al., 2004), leading to robust regulation of enzyme activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Johnson et al., 1996 and Nolen et al., 2004.

claim: Phosphorylation of the TxY motif in ERK1 and ERK2 can lead to a 1000-fold increase in activity (Zhang et al., 1994; Canagarajah et al., 1997; Roskoski, 2012).
source: Together, these conformational changes can lead to a 1000-fold increase in activity (Zhang et al., 1994; Canagarajah et al., 1997; Roskoski, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Zhang et al., 1994, Canagarajah et al., 1997, and Roskoski, 2012.

claim: ERK1 and ERK2 exhibit very low autophosphorylation activity as purified proteins in vitro (Levin-Salomon et al., 2008; Beenstock et al., 2014).
source: The MAP kinases ERK1 and ERK2 exhibit very low autophosphorylation activity as purified proteins in vitro (Levin-Salomon et al., 2008; Beenstock et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Levin-Salomon et al., 2008 and Beenstock et al., 2014.

claim: ERK1 and ERK2 manifest high activity in vivo only when they are phosphorylated by the upstream MAPKK, MAP/ERK kinase (MEK).
source: and they manifest high activity in vivo only when they are phosphorylated by the upstream MAPKK, MAP/ERK kinase (MEK).
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about ERK regulation.

claim: An ERK1 mutant with high autophosphorylation activity can drive oncogenic transformation of cells (Smorodinsky-Atias et al., 2016).
source: and one such mutant can drive oncogenic transformation of cells (Smorodinsky-Atias et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Smorodinsky-Atias et al., 2016.

claim: An inferred deep ancestor of the CMGC group had high basal activity even in the absence of any activating kinase or allosteric activators.
source: As part of this study, we observed that an inferred deep ancestor of this group had high basal activity even in the absence of any activating kinase or allosteric activators.
evidence: This is a finding from the previous study by Howard et al., 2014, referenced in the text.

claim: Within the p38 subfamilies, p38β has a much higher basal catalytic activity than p38α (Beenstock et al., 2014).
source: For example, within the p38 subfamilies, p38β has a much higher basal catalytic activity than p38α (Beenstock et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Beenstock et al., 2014.

claim: ERK7 is constitutively active (Abe et al., 1999; Abe et al., 2001).
source: and within the ERK family, ERK7 is constitutively active (Abe et al., 1999; Abe et al., 2001)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Abe et al., 1999 and Abe et al., 2001.

claim: The core kinase domain of ERK5 has a much higher autophosphorylation rate than ERK1 and ERK2 (Buschbeck and Ullrich, 2005).
source: and the core kinase domain of ERK5 has a much higher autophosphorylation rate, and thus higher basal activity, than ERK1 and ERK2, which are almost completely inactive in the absence of the activating kinase MEK (Buschbeck and Ullrich, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Buschbeck and Ullrich, 2005.

claim: The transition to dependence on MEK occurred between the inferred common ancestor of ERK1, 2 and 5, and that of ERK1 and 2.
source: Through biochemical analysis of reconstructed kinases, we found that the transition to dependence on MEK occurred between the inferred common ancestor of ERK1, 2 and 5, and that of ERK1 and 2.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: Two changes—mutation of the gatekeeper residue and a single amino acid deletion in the linker loop between the β3 strand and αC helix—accounted for the regulatory evolution from high to low autophosphorylation.
source: Two changes— mutation of the gatekeeper residue and a single amino acid deletion in the linker loop between the β3 strand and αC helix accounted for this regulatory evolution.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: Reversal of the inferred evolutionary mutations in modern ERK1 and ERK2 led to full autoactivation in the absence of an upstream activating kinase.
source: Reversal of these inferred evolutionary mutations in modern ERK1 and ERK2 led to full autoactivation in the absence of an upstream activating kinase.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: Sequences sampled for each kinase family were selected to be evenly distributed across the eukaryotic phylogeny.
source: The sequences sampled for each kinase family were selected to be evenly distributed across the eukaryotic phylogeny.
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: A maximum likelihood phylogenetic method was used to infer the sequences of the ancestral kinases (Hanson-Smith and Johnson, 2016).
source: We then used a maximum likelihood phylogenetic method (Hanson-Smith and Johnson, 2016) to infer the sequences of the ancestral kinases
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study, with a citation to the method.

claim: The inferred ancestor of all MAP kinases (AncMAPK) had a strong preference for proline at the +1 position.
source: All inferred ancestors had a strong preference for proline at the +1 position including the inferred ancestor of all MAP kinases (AncMAPK, Figure 1B), as expected.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from positional scanning peptide libraries shown in Figure 1B.

claim: All inferred ancestors prior to and including AncERK1-5 had relatively high activity, while AncERK1-2 had low activity, almost comparable to modern ERK1/2.
source: We found that all inferred ancestors prior to and including AncERK1-5 had relatively high activity, while AncERK1-2 had low activity, almost comparable to modern ERK1/2 (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by kinase activity assays shown in Figure 1C.

claim: AncERK1-2 was activated ~6 fold either by coincubation with MEK or by purification from an E. coli strain that coexpressed MEK.
source: Importantly, AncERK1-2 was activated ~6 fold either by coincubation with MEK (Figure 1C) or by purification from an E. coli strain that coexpressed MEK (Figure 1—figure supplement 5C and D)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 5C and D.

claim: The decrease in activity of AncERK1-2 was due to both an increase in the Michaelis-Menten constant (KM) and a decrease in kcat.
source: The decrease in activity of AncERK1-2 was due to both an increase in the Michaelis-Menten constant (KM) and a decrease in kcat (Table 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is supported by kinetic data presented in Table 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: Mutation of the 'TxY' motif to 'AxF' greatly reduced the activity of all inferred kinase ancestors.
source: These mutations greatly reduced the activity of all inferred kinase ancestors (Figure 2B)
evidence: This is supported by kinase activity assays shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The level of phosphorylated tyrosine (Tx-pY) was relatively high in deeper inferred ancestors and dropped precipitously at the transition to AncERK1-2.
source: Consistent with the kinase activity transition, we observed that the level of phosphorylated tyrosine (Tx-pY) was relatively high in deeper inferred ancestors: AncCDK.MAPK (22.9%), AncMAPK (32.3%), AncJPE (48.1%), AncERK (76.3%) and AncERK1-5 (76.0%), and then dropped precipitously at the transition to AncERK1-2 (5.7%), which had levels similar to modern Erk1 (3.8%).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS quantification data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Di-phosphorylation of the 'TxY' motif (pT-x-pY) was detected in the inferred deep ancestor kinases AncCDK.MAPK (6.3%), AncJPE (27.6%) and AncERK (7.9%).
source: Notably, we also detected di-phosphorylation of the 'TxY' motif (pT-x-pY) in the inferred deep ancestor kinases AncCDK.MAPK (6.3%), AncJPE (27.6%) and AncERK (7.9%).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS quantification data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Alternative inferred ancestors combining all alternate residues with posterior probability >0.2 behaved similarly to the original inferred ancestors.
source: The inferred ancestors of alternative kinases behaved similarly to the original inferred ancestors (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by kinase activity assays shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Reverting two amino acids (ins44R and Q89M) to the inferred ancestral state in AncERK1-2 was sufficient to confer high basal activity to this kinase.
source: Indeed, reverting these amino acids to the inferred ancestral state in AncERK1-2 (referred to as the AncERK1-2-ins44R-Q89M mutant) was sufficient to confer high basal activity to this kinase (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by kinase activity assays shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The 44R insertion maps to the loop between the β3 strand and helix αC, and the Q89M mutation maps to the gatekeeper position at the back of the ATP-binding pocket.
source: By modeling the AncERK1-2 sequence onto the Erk2 structure (PDB: 1ERK), we mapped the 44R insertion to the loop between the β3 strand and helix αC, and the Q89M mutation to the gatekeeper position at the back of the ATP-binding pocket (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by structural modeling shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The insertion mutation in the β3-αC loop increased ERK1 activity more than 30-fold.
source: The insertion increased ERK1 activity more than 30-fold (Figure 4A; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by kinase activity assays shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Q122M gatekeeper mutant led to ERK1 activation.
source: We also found that the Q122M gatekeeper mutant led to ERK1 activation (Figure 4A)
evidence: This is supported by kinase activity assays shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The combination of the loop insertion and Q122M gatekeeper mutation raised ERK1 activity by more than 2 orders of magnitude.
source: Indeed, the combination of these two mutations raised ERK1 activity by more than 2 orders of magnitude, almost to the levels of ERK1 after activation with MEK.
evidence: This is supported by kinase activity assays shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Loop length from K72 to P75 is important in the determination of ERK1 basal activity.
source: These results confirmed the importance of loop length from K72 to P75 in the determination of ERK1 basal activity.
evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Mutations in the 'TxY' motif to 'AxY', 'TxF' and 'AxF' all abolished the increased activity caused by the insertion mutation.
source: Consistent with this idea, mutations in this motif to 'AxY', 'TxF' and 'AxF' all abolished the increased activity caused by the insertion mutation (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by kinase activity assays shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Western blots and LC-MS quantification showed elevated 'TxY' phosphorylation in mutant kinases.
source: Furthermore, Western blots using an antibody specific for phosphorylated ERK (Figure 4B) and LC-MS quantification of tryptic peptides (Figure 4D) both showed elevated 'TxY' phosphorylation in mutant kinases.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 4B and LC-MS data in Figure 4D.

claim: Autophosphorylation rates were increased in the ERK1-ins74N mutant.
source: Indeed, experiments incubating kinase with ATP-y-32P in the absence of substrate showed that autophosphorylation rates were indeed increased in the ERK1-ins74N mutant (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by autophosphorylation assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Autophosphorylation scales linearly with ERK1 concentration, indicating a cis-autophosphorylation mechanism.
source: We found the former result to be true (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by concentration-dependent autophosphorylation data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: The evolutionary mutations identified in ERK1 also led to activation of ERK2.
source: First, we confirmed that the evolutionary mutations identified in ERK1 also led to activation of ERK2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by kinase activity assays shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: ERK2-ins55N showed increased flexibility at the glycine rich loop.
source: ERK2-ins55N showed increased flexibility at the glycine rich loop (Figure 5B)
evidence: This is supported by RMSF analysis from MD simulations shown in Figure 5B.

claim: ERK2-Q103M showed increased flexibility at loop 16 (L16).
source: ERK2-Q103M showed increased flexibility at loop 16 (L16, Figure 5C)
evidence: This is supported by RMSF analysis from MD simulations shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The ERK2-ins55N-Q103M double mutant was more flexible at both the glycine rich loop and L16.
source: and the ERK2-ins55N-Q103M double mutant was more flexible at both the glycine rich loop and L16 (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by RMSF analysis from MD simulations shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The K52-E69 salt bridge was more frequently present in mutants than WT.
source: Indeed, the K52-E69 salt bridge was more frequently present in mutants than WT (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by distance analysis from MD simulations shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Average inter-residue distances K52-D165 and E69-F166 were significantly reduced in at least one of the mutants.
source: Here, average inter-residue distances were significantly reduced in at least one of the mutants (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A and B).
evidence: This is supported by distance analysis from MD simulations shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A and B.

claim: The evolutionary mutation led to MEK-independent ERK1 activity in vivo.
source: This result suggests that the evolutionary mutation led to MEK-independent ERK1 activity in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by ERK-KTR reporter assays shown in Figure 6B and C.

claim: Cells expressing ERK1-ins74N exhibited robust phosphorylation after treatment with Trametinib.
source: The western blot result showed that the phosphorylation level of 'TEY' motif in wild type ERK1 was very low after treatment with Trametinib, while the cells expressing ERK1-ins74N exhibited robust phosphorylation (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Changes in the β3-αC loop length of BRAF, EGFR, and HER2 led to activation of these kinases (Foster et al., 2016).
source: It has recently been discovered that changes in the β3-αC loop length of BRAF, EGFR, and HER2, none of which are in the CMGC group of kinases, also led to activation of these kinases (Foster et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Foster et al., 2016.

claim: The inferred deep ancestor of the CMGC group contained hallmarks of specificity found along multiple branches of the CMGC phylogenetic tree including +1 proline, −2 proline and −3 arginine preference.
source: As previously reported, the inferred deep ancestor of the CMGC group contained hallmarks of specificity found along multiple branches of the CMGC phylogenetic tree including +1 proline, −2 proline and −3 arginine preference.
evidence: This is a finding from a previous study, referenced in the text.

claim: The new inferred CDK and MAPK ancestors lost the −3 arginine specificity at the transition to the inferred ancestor of CDK and MAPK (AncCDK.MAPK).
source: The new inferred CDK and MAPK ancestors generated for the current study lost the −3 arginine specificity at the transition to the inferred ancestor of CDK and MAPK (AncCDK.MAPK, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and B).
evidence: This is supported by PSPL specificity data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and B.

claim: The loss of −3 arginine specificity was most likely due to the mutation of Glu to Ser in the conserved HRDxKPEN motif.
source: This was most likely due to the mutation of Glu to Ser in the conserved HRDxKPEN motif, previously reported to be a strong determinant of −3 arginine preference (Mok et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an inference based on previous findings cited from Mok et al., 2010.

claim: AncERK1-2 had much lower activity towards ELK1 than AncERK1-5.
source: AncERK1-2 also had had much lower activity towards EL-1 than AncERK1-5 (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A and B)
evidence: This is supported by kinase activity assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5A and B.

claim: The modest activation of AncERK1-2 by MEK is likely due to the high specificity of MEK for ERK1 and 2.
source: We believe that the modest activation of AncERK1-2 by MEK is due to the high specificity this activating kinase; AncERK1-2 is likely a poor MEK substrate compared to modern ERKs 1 and 2.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed data.

claim: Chimeras that swapped the middle domain of the inferred ancestors had no effect on activity.
source: However, chimeras that swapped the middle domain of the inferred ancestors had no effect on activity.
evidence: This is supported by chimera analysis data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Changes in the N-terminus were responsible for most of the difference in the activity of the inferred ancestors.
source: Rather, our initial chimeras indicated that changes in the N-terminus were responsible for most of the difference in the activity of these inferred ancestors (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is supported by chimera analysis data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Introducing the two mutations (deletion of R46 and mutation of M90 to Q) into AncERK1-5 suppressed basal activity to the levels of AncERK1-2.
source: Conversely, introducing just these two mutations into AncERK1-5 (i.e. deletion of R46 and mutation of M90 to Q) suppressed basal activity to the levels of AncERK1-2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C and E).
evidence: This is supported by kinase activity assays shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C and E.

claim: All the inferred ancestors prior to AncERK1-2 had a longer linker loop and a hydrophobic residue at the gatekeeper position.
source: All the inferred ancestors prior to AncERK1-2 had a longer linker loop and a hydrophobic residue at the gatekeeper position (Figure 3C; Figure 3—figure supplements 3 and 4).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplements 3 and 4.

claim: Mutation in the gatekeeper residue has been reported to activate ERK2 in previous studies (Emrick et al., 2006).
source: Mutation in the gatekeeper residue has been reported to activate ERK2 in previous studies (Emrick et al., 2006)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Emrick et al., 2006.

claim: Many amino acid insertions at position 74 in ERK1 increased kinase activity.
source: Indeed, we found that, in addition to arginine and asparagine, many other amino acid insertions also increased ERK1 activity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Deletions and insertions from K72 to P75 greatly affected mutant activity.
source: Deletions and insertions from K72 to P75 (ERK1 numbering) greatly affected mutant activity.
evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: Length changes after P75 had a minor effect on activity.
source: However, length changes after P75, had a minor effect (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: The E. coli bacterium used to express ERK1 and inferred ancestral kinases lacks endogenous kinases capable of phosphorylating the 'TxY' motif.
source: The E. coli bacterium that we use to express ERK1 and inferred ancestral kinases lacks endogenous kinases capable of phosphorylating the 'TxY' motif.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about E. coli.

claim: The increased phosphorylation of 'TEY' motif is likely caused by autophosphorylation (Howard et al., 2014).
source: Therefore, the increased phosphorylation of 'TEY' motif is likely caused by autophosphorylation (Howard et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental system and previous findings cited from Howard et al., 2014.

claim: 1000 independent MD simulations were performed on Folding@home for ERK2-WT, ins55N, Q103M and the ins55N-Q103M double mutant.
source: We performed 1000 independent MD simulations on Folding@home (Shirts and Pande, 2000) for ERK2- WT, ins55N, Q103M and the ins55N-Q103M double mutant starting from the unphosphorylated ERK2 structure (PDBID: 1ERK)
evidence: This describes the computational methodology used in the study.

claim: The 4,000 MD simulations were propagated for a total of at least 500 μs per system, resulting in an aggregate total of ~2.05 ms of simulation time.
source: These 4,000 MD simulations were propagated for a total of at least 500 μs per system, resulting in an aggregate total of ~2.05 ms of simulation time (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This describes the computational methodology used in the study.

claim: The frequency of conformations where Y185 is hydrogen bonded to D147 is highest in WT (1.7%) and decreases for the mutants.
source: Unexpectedly, the frequency of these conformations is the highest in WT (1.7%) and decreases for the mutants (0.9% for 55N, 0.4% for Q103M, and 0.2% for 55N-Q103M) (Figure 5G, which shows only D147-Y185 distances of <4 Å).
evidence: This is supported by distance analysis from MD simulations shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Seven residues had absolute mean contact changes larger than 0.05 with Y185: L168, R192, I196, K201, G202, I207, and Y231.
source: For all three mutants, the same seven residues had absolute mean contact changes larger than 0.05: L168, R192, I196, K201, G202, I207, and Y231.
evidence: This is supported by contact analysis from MD simulations shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 7.

claim: Cells expressing ERK1-ins74N had significantly more ERK-KTR in the cytoplasm compared to cells expressing ERK1-WT.
source: In contrast, cells expressing ERK1-ins74N had significantly more ERK-KTR in the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6B and C.

claim: The Ras/RAF/MEK/ERK pathway is one of the most important signaling axes in oncogenesis.
source: Indeed, the Ras/RAF/MEK/ERK pathway is one of the most important signaling axes in oncogenesis.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge in cancer biology.

claim: ERK is not simply an ON/OFF switch, but rather oscillates or adapts in various contexts (Albeck et al., 2013).
source: ERK is not simply an ON/OFF switch, but rather oscillates or adapts in various contexts (Albeck et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Albeck et al., 2013.

claim: The evolutionary changes that place ERKs 1 and 2 under stringent regulation synergize in their effects.
source: We found that the evolutionary changes that place ERKs 1 and 2 under stringent regulation synergize in their effects.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: The gatekeeper mutation has been previously described as an activating mutation (Emrick et al., 2006; Azam et al., 2008).
source: One change, a polar substitution in the 'gatekeeper' residue of the active site has been previously described as an activating mutation (Emrick et al., 2006; Azam et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Emrick et al., 2006 and Azam et al., 2008.

claim: The permissive methionine residue at the gatekeeper was retained along the branch that led to the modern ERK5 family.
source: The permissive methionine residue was retained along the branch that led to the modern ERK5 family, which also has high rates of autophosphorylation.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis and kinase activity data.

claim: In ERK1-2 the gatekeeper was shifted to glutamine, a more restrictive state for autoactivation.
source: In ERK1-2 the gatekeeper was shifted to glutamine, a more restrictive state for autoactivation.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis and kinase activity data.

claim: The inferred deeper CMGC ancestors and the modern ERK kinases that have higher basal activity, ERK5 and ERK7, all had one extra amino acid in the β3-αC loop.
source: The inferred deeper CMGC ancestors and the modern ERK kinases that have higher basal activity, ERK5 and ERK7, all had one extra amino acid in this loop (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Each of the two evolutionary changes confers an order of magnitude change in basal activity.
source: Each of these evolutionary changes confers an order of magnitude change in basal activity, and when combined, these two mutations increase the basal activity of ERKs 1 and 2 by more than two orders of magnitude.
evidence: This is supported by kinase activity assays.

claim: Reversion to a more active inferred ancestral state increased flexibility in the glycine rich loop and loop 16.
source: First, there was increased flexibility in the glycine rich loop and loop 16 (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is supported by RMSF analysis from MD simulations shown in Figure 5A–C.

claim: The reorganization of loop 16 is important in the domain closure of kinases.
source: The reorganization of loop 16 is important in the domain closure of kinases, which is an intrinsic part of the conformational shift to an active state.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge in kinase biology.

claim: Gatekeeper mutations can increase domain closure (Barr et al., 2011).
source: This observation is consistent with earlier MD simulations that showed that gatekeeper mutations can increase domain closure (Barr et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Barr et al., 2011.

claim: The active site is more likely to attain a productive conformation in mutants, as indicated by more frequent formation of the K52-E69 salt-bridge.
source: The most compelling hypothesis suggested by our MD simulations was that the active site is more likely to attain a productive conformation in mutants, as indicated by more frequent formation of the K52-E69 salt-bridge in mutants than wild type (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by distance analysis from MD simulations shown in Figure 5D (which is actually Figure 5E in the manuscript).

claim: Changes in hormone-receptor ligand binding domain specificity required stabilizing mutations prior to the advent of mutations that alter specificity (Thornton et al., 2003).
source: For example, changes in the specificity of hormone-receptor ligand binding domains required stabilizing mutations (Thornton et al., 2003) prior to the advent of mutations that alter specificity
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Thornton et al., 2003.

claim: The acquisition of novel mutations after acquisition of a new function made it difficult to revert to the inferred ancestral state (Bridgham et al., 2009).
source: and the acquisition of novel mutations after acquisition of a new function made it difficult to revert to the inferred ancestral state (Bridgham et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bridgham et al., 2009.

claim: In the previous study on the evolution of kinase specificity, no requirement for stabilizing mutations was found.
source: In our previous study on the evolution of kinase specificity, we found no requirement for stabilizing mutations – robust activity was maintained as specificity changed.
evidence: This is a finding from a previous study by the authors.

claim: The reversion of a single or double evolutionary mutation is well tolerated in kinases.
source: In the current study, we find that the reversion of a single or double evolutionary mutation is also well tolerated
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: Modern ERK1 and ERK2 can be reverted to an inferred ancestral state of high basal activity without a strong evolutionary ratchet.
source: and that we can revert modern ERK1 and ERK2 to an inferred ancestral state of high basal activity - there is not a strong "evolutionary ratchet".
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: Kinases are quite tolerant of mutations.
source: Together these observations suggest that kinases are quite tolerant of mutations, which perhaps explains their frequent dysregulation in diseases like cancer.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings of the study.

claim: The 'evolvability' of kinases may explain the prevalence of kinases as regulatory enzymes in Eukaryotes.
source: Perhaps this 'evolvability' explains the prevalence of kinases as regulatory enzymes in Eukaryotes.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings of the study.
